name: Hortobágy National Park - the Puszta
blurb: Alkaline puszta where grazing herds, ground squirrels and falcons share open steppe.

tip.title: Remove the ground squirrels
tip.text: Ground squirrels feed saker falcons and foxes. Set European ground squirrel to -100% and watch the saker falcon, then foxes turning to other prey such as bustards.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Hortobágy National Park - the Puszta

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Hortobágy National Park, Great bustard, European ground squirrel). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Summer sun powers the open, treeless grassland and the shallow wetlands that make up the puszta.
Fungi, bacteria and soil invertebrates break down dung, dead grass and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Puszta grasses
nodes.desc: Short, hardy grasses and herbs of the alkaline pastures; they feed the grazers and are kept short by them.
Reed beds line the marshes and fishponds, giving food and cover to geese, herons and harriers.

nodes.name: Hungarian Grey cattle
nodes.desc: A hardy landrace long herded on the puszta by mounted csikos. Grazing keeps the pasture open and short.
A large water frog of ponds and canals that eats insects and other small animals and is food for herons, snakes and eagles.
A wading bird that spears frogs, snakes and small mammals at the edges of fishponds and in wet grassland.
A raptor of reed beds that hunts frogs, snakes and small mammals over wetlands and nearby fields.
A generalist that takes rodents, ground squirrels, birds and their eggs, frogs and carrion.
A huge eagle around the fishponds and marshes that takes waterbirds, mammals and amphibians and also eats carrion.

story: Hortobágy in eastern Hungary is an 800 km² national park, the country's first, designated in 1973. It is the largest semi-natural grassland in Europe. It joined the World Heritage List in 1999 for its more than four thousand years of pastoral culture.
matters: Its alkaline steppe is far older than once believed: alkalinization began around ten thousand years ago, when the Tisza cut through the Great Hungarian Plain. Grazing animals then finished shaping it.
